title: Wispy dark clouds
caption: The dark nebulae Barnard 92 and Barnard 93, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
credit: ESO/VPHAS+ team. Acknowledgement: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two dark, wispy clouds hang against a field of stars, like ghostly trails in the sky. They are Barnard 92, on the right, and Barnard 93, on the left, two dark nebulae photographed from ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Their inky darkness comes from thick gas and dust that block the light of the stars behind. That darkness hides activity, because these clouds are stellar nurseries, where collapsing gas and dust give birth to new stars.

The rich starry backdrop is part of a much larger complex, the Small Sagittarius Star Cloud, also cataloged by Charles Messier as Messier 24. This part of the sky, in the constellation Sagittarius, is so crowded with stars that it can be seen with the naked eye on dark nights.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM camera took this visible-light image through g, r and i filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The color mapping isn't published.
filters: 480 nm · Optical g (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
625 nm · Optical r (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
659 nm · Optical H-alpha (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
770 nm · Optical i (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
understand.eye: The star cloud is visible to the naked eye on dark nights, but the camera records far more stars and detail than the eye could.

explore: The image was taken with OmegaCAM, a 268-million-pixel camera on the VLT Survey Telescope designed for wide fields. This field could hold four full Moons. It is part of the VPHAS+ survey, which has mapped diffuse nebulae and both young and evolved stars in our galaxy.
